slides.title: Total cholesterol determination. Clinical diagnostic significance
bullets: Clinical biochemistry and biochemical testing methods
Practical session — 6 h

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Tests: Total cholesterol; HDL cholesterol; LDL cholesterol; Non-HDL cholesterol
Conditions: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
Reference values: Reference values and decision limits
Practice: Q&A: 12 + 3

slides.title: Total cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: A cholesterol test (lipid panel) gives information about the risk of developing heart disease. It reports LDL, HDL, total cholesterol and triglycerides; total cholesterol is the overall amount of cholesterol in the blood and includes HDL and LDL cholesterol.

The test may be ordered as part of a routine exam; when and how often depends on age, risk factors and family history. It may be done more often with a high risk of heart problems, such as a family history of heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, smoking, excess weight, lack of physical activity or a diet high in saturated fat.

slides.title: Total cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance present in the blood and in every cell. The body uses it to make hormones, vitamin D and substances that help digest food; the liver makes all the cholesterol the body needs and removes the excess, and more comes from animal-source foods.

slides.title: Total cholesterol
bullets: High: High cholesterol can lead to heart disease. Factors the source links to higher cholesterol include foods high in saturated fat and cholesterol, excess weight, stress (through hormones such as corticosteroids) and drinking too much alcohol, which can raise total cholesterol; age and genes also play a role.

High: Inherited gene changes can cause familial hypercholesterolemia. Conditions associated with a risk of high cholesterol include chronic kidney disease, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, hypothyroidism, lupus, overweight and obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome and sleep apnea.

slides.title: Total cholesterol
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting (no food or drink) for 9 to 12 hours may be required, which is why the test is often done in the morning. The provider says whether fasting or other special instructions apply.

Limitations: A healthy cholesterol level for a given person may depend on age, family history, lifestyle and other heart-disease risk factors such as high triglycerides. Which numbers suit an individual is discussed with the provider.

slides.title: HDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: HDL is one of the values reported in a cholesterol test, which is used to assess the risk of heart disease. HDL helps get rid of “bad” LDL cholesterol, and a higher HDL level may help reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke.

Physiology: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is a lipoprotein, a combination of fat and protein that lets lipids travel in the blood. It is called “good” cholesterol because it carries cholesterol from other parts of the body back to the liver, which then removes it from the body.

slides.title: HDL cholesterol
bullets: High: For HDL, higher numbers are generally better, because a high HDL level can lower the risk of coronary artery disease and stroke. In general, low LDL together with high HDL is considered good for heart health.
Low: An unhealthy lifestyle is the most common cause of low HDL. Smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke can lower HDL, and weight gain (including from too much alcohol) lowers it as well.
Low: Certain medicines can lower HDL in some people, including beta blockers, anabolic steroids (including testosterone), progestins and benzodiazepines. Diabetes can also lower HDL.

slides.title: HDL cholesterol
bullets: Pre-analytics: HDL is measured in the cholesterol test, which may require fasting (no food or drink) for 9 to 12 hours; the provider says whether this is needed.

Limitations: How high HDL should be depends on age and sex. NHLBI cites a study that found higher HDL may not be as beneficial in some Black and White adults as was once believed; other risk factors such as high blood pressure, obesity or diabetes may outweigh its benefits.

slides.title: LDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L
What it is used for: LDL is measured as part of a cholesterol test that helps assess heart-disease risk. The source describes LDL cholesterol as the main source of blockages in the arteries.

Physiology: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) is called “bad” cholesterol because a high LDL level leads to cholesterol buildup in the arteries. Excess LDL together with other substances forms plaque (atherosclerosis); in the heart arteries this narrows them and can cause angina or a heart attack.

slides.title: LDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · Reference values and decision limits · 1/2
rows: Coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk equivalents (10-year CHD risk above 20%)
2 or more risk factors (10-year risk 20% or lower)
High risk: CHD or CHD risk equivalents (10-year risk above 20%)
Moderately high risk: 2 or more risk factors (10-year risk 10–20%)
Moderate risk: 2 or more risk factors (10-year risk below 10%)

slides.title: LDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · Reference values and decision limits · 2/2
rows: High or moderately high risk, when LDL-lowering drug therapy is used
≥ 50% reduction from baseline and < 1.4 mmol/L (< 55 mg/dL)
Very high risk (primary or secondary prevention)
≥ 50% reduction from baseline and < 1.8 mmol/L (< 70 mg/dL)
Patients with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
Very high-risk ASCVD, on maximal statin therapy
LDL-C reduction of ≥ 30%; if 10-year risk is ≥ 20%, ≥ 50%
Primary prevention: age 40–75, no diabetes, LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL, when a statin is indicated

slides.title: LDL cholesterol
bullets: High: Factors that can raise LDL include a diet high in saturated fat and cholesterol, excess weight, lack of physical activity and smoking (which lowers HDL). Cholesterol levels rise with age, and in women LDL tends to rise after menopause; genes also play a part, as in familial hypercholesterolemia.

High: Certain medicines (for example steroids, some blood pressure medicines and HIV medicines) and diseases such as chronic kidney disease, diabetes and HIV can raise LDL. NHLBI also lists amiodarone, beta-blockers, chemotherapy, thiazide diuretics, cyclosporine, retinoids and prednisone among medicines that can raise LDL or lower HDL.
Low: For LDL, lower numbers are better, because a high LDL level can raise the risk of coronary artery disease and related problems.

slides.title: LDL cholesterol
bullets: Pre-analytics: LDL is measured in the cholesterol test, which may require fasting (no food or drink) for 9 to 12 hours; the provider says whether this is needed.
Limitations: An LDL result marked “calculated” is an estimate based on total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides. LDL may also be measured “directly” in the blood sample.
LDL goals are individual. With coronary artery disease or high risk, the provider may set different LDL goals, using a risk estimator (PREVENT) that considers age, health history and family history.

slides.title: Non-HDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L
What it is used for: Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol; it may be reported with lipid (lipoprotein) panel results.
Non-HDL includes LDL and other types of cholesterol such as VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein), so it gives a better picture of all the “bad” cholesterol types that can raise heart risk.

slides.title: Non-HDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · Reference values and decision limits
rows: Coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk equivalents (10-year CHD risk above 20%)
2 or more risk factors (10-year risk 20% or lower)
Very high risk with high triglycerides

slides.title: Non-HDL cholesterol
bullets: Limitations: The numbers that are best for a person may depend on age, race, blood pressure, weight, family history and more, so the lipid levels that are best for them are checked with the provider.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: High cholesterol is found from medical and family history, a physical exam and a blood test (lipid panel). Screening in healthy people: start at ages 9–11 and repeat every 5 years; every 5 years at 20–65 (every 1–2 years for men 45–65 and women 55–65); yearly after 65.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: The main source of cholesterol buildup and blockages in arteries; high LDL raises risk.
Helps decrease cholesterol blockages in arteries; low HDL is a concern.
High triglycerides may signal a higher risk of coronary heart disease.
The main screening test is a lipid panel; fasting for 8–12 hours may be requested.
Total cholesterol minus HDL; may also be reported.
Not part of a routine lipid panel; largely inherited and stable over life. May be ordered with a family history of stroke or early heart disease, or if family history is unknown.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: Higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
HDL < 40 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) in men or < 50 mg/dL (≈1.3 mmol/L) in women
May mean a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease; may lead to a statin prescription.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: Individual target levels are set by the clinician based on risk factors. mmol/L values are converted from mg/dL (approximate).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: very high risk <1.4 (and a reduction of ≥50%); high <1.8; moderate <2.6; low <3.0 mmol/L
Lp(a) – inherited very high level (ESC/EAS 2019 guideline)

Recommendation of section 5.5: ≥180 mg/dL (≥430 nmol/L) – identify by measuring at least once in a lifetime; in the text of section 5.3.4 >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – increased lifetime ASCVD risk (the source differs between "≥" and ">"). This is not a universal norm or a single risk threshold mg/dL (nmol/L value from the source itself; conversion depends on the assay)

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: rule-out <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L); gray zone 30–50 mg/dL (75–125 nmol/L) – assessed together with other risk factors; rule-in >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L) (in the concluding item "≥50 mg/dL; 125 nmol/L") mg/dL and nmol/L separately (a standard conversion factor is not recommended; 2–2.5 is only an estimate)
EAS consensus statement 2022 (Kronenberg et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3925)
Lp(a) – lifetime risk equivalent to HeFH
>180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – lifetime ASCVD risk equivalent to untreated heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia mg/dL (nmol/L from the source)
Applicability limit of the Friedewald formula
LDL = TC − HDL − TG/2.2 (mmol/L) or TG/5 (mg/dL); not used when TG >4.5 mmol/L (>400 mg/dL) mmol/L

slides.title: In a lipid panel, what does total cholesterol represent?
options: Only the LDL cholesterol, without the HDL fraction
The overall amount of cholesterol in the blood, including HDL and LDL
The total amount of fat in the blood, including triglycerides and cholesterol
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source describes total cholesterol as the total amount of cholesterol in the blood, including HDL and LDL cholesterol.

Basis: MedlinePlus: total cholesterol is the total amount of cholesterol in the blood and includes HDL and LDL cholesterol.

slides.title: A patient asks for the one total cholesterol value that is healthy for everyone. Which answer best reflects the source?
options: A healthy level may depend on age, family history, lifestyle and other risk factors, so it is discussed with the provider
A single cutoff applies to all people regardless of risk
Only the laboratory method determines what is healthy for the person
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says a healthy level for a person may depend on these factors and that the provider explains what is right for them.

Basis: MedlinePlus: a healthy cholesterol level for a person may depend on age, family history, lifestyle and other risk factors.

slides.title: Why is HDL often called “good” cholesterol?
options: It carries cholesterol away from the liver and delivers it to the arteries and other tissues
It is a type of fat stored in fat cells, which the body uses for energy
It carries cholesterol from other parts of the body back to the liver, which removes it
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is how the source explains why HDL is called “good”.

Basis: MedlinePlus: HDL carries cholesterol from other parts of the body back to the liver, which removes it from the body.

slides.title: A patient has a low HDL result. Which factor does the source list as able to lower HDL?
options: Regular aerobic exercise done several times each week
Smoking or certain medicines such as beta blockers
Losing excess weight through diet and exercise
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says smoking, secondhand smoke and certain medicines such as beta blockers can lower HDL.

Basis: MedlinePlus: smoking, secondhand smoke and certain medicines (e.g. beta blockers) can lower HDL; exercise and weight loss can raise it.

slides.title: An LDL result on a report is marked “calculated”. What does this mean?
options: LDL was measured directly in the sample, not estimated from other values
It is an estimate based on total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides
The sample was analyzed twice and the two LDL results were averaged
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says a “calculated” LDL is an estimate based on total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides.

Basis: MedlinePlus: a “calculated” LDL is an estimate based on total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides; LDL may also be measured directly.

slides.title: Two patients have the same LDL value, but one has coronary artery disease. Why might their LDL goals differ?
options: Because LDL goals depend only on the laboratory method
They cannot differ; one LDL goal applies to every adult
Goals depend on individual risk: with coronary artery disease or high risk, the provider may set different LDL goals
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is what the source states.

Basis: MedlinePlus: with coronary artery disease or a high risk of it, the provider may have different LDL goals.

slides.title: A 40-year-old patient, plasma is clear, cholesterol 7.3 mmol/L, HDL-C 0.88 mmol/L, atherogenic index 7.1. How do you assess the lipid profile:
Disorders of lipid metabolism. Atherosclerosis?
bullets: 1. Disorders of lipid metabolism: primary (inherited – familial hypercholesterolemia, familial hyperchylomicronemia – LPL or apoC-II deficiency, etc.) and secondary (diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, obesity, alcohol, drugs).

2. Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis: apoB-containing lipoproteins (mainly LDL) are retained in the vessel intima and oxidized → macrophages become foam cells → inflammation, plaque; LDL and other apoB-containing lipoproteins are a direct cause of ASCVD.

slides.title: Disorders of lipid metabolism. Atherosclerosis?
bullets: 3. Laboratory assessment: total cholesterol, TG, HDL, LDL (calculated or direct), non-HDL cholesterol, apoB (fasting not required), Lp(a) – a risk modifier: measure at least once in adults; EAS 2022 consensus: <30 mg/dL (<75 nmol/L) – risk excluded, 30–50 mg/dL – gray zone, >50 mg/dL (>125 nmol/L) – risk confirmed; >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) – lifetime risk equivalent to HeFH; ESC/EAS 2019: inherited very high level ≥180 mg/dL (≥430 nmol/L). There is no universal "normal" for Lp(a); mg/dL↔nmol/L conversion depends on the assay.
4. Target values depend on the overall cardiovascular risk (ESC/EAS 2019: in very high risk LDL <1.4 mmol/L).
5. Fredrickson (WHO) classification: I (chylomicrons), IIa (LDL), IIb (LDL + VLDL), III (remnants), IV (VLDL), V (chylomicrons + VLDL) – a historical phenotype classification.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of determining total cholesterol, calculating the atherogenic index?
bullets: 1. Determination of total cholesterol: enzymatic method (cholesterol esterase → cholesterol oxidase → H2O2 + peroxidase/4-aminophenazone, Trinder reaction) – the standard on automated analyzers.

2. Clinical significance: alone it estimates risk poorly – together with HDL, LDL, TG; increase – primary hypercholesterolemia, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, pregnancy; decrease – severe liver disease, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, emaciation.
3. Non-HDL cholesterol = total cholesterol − HDL – reflects all atherogenic lipoproteins, fasting not required; a secondary target in modern guidelines.
4. The "atherogenic index" (total cholesterol − HDL)/HDL – used in regional practice; in international guidelines risk is assessed by LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, apoB and an overall risk score.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of determining total cholesterol, calculating the atherogenic index?
bullets: 5. Preanalytics: for a lipid profile fasting is usually not required (repeat fasting if TG is very high); the result may change after an acute illness.

slides.title: Lipoprotein metabolism and atherosclerosis?
bullets: 1. Exogenous pathway: in the intestine chylomicrons (apoB-48) → TG are removed by LPL → chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver via apoE.
2. Endogenous pathway: the liver secretes VLDL (apoB-100) → with LPL IDL → LDL; LDL delivers cholesterol to the tissues via LDL receptors.
3. Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL (apoA-I) takes cholesterol from peripheral tissues and returns it to the liver.
4. Atherosclerosis: retention of apoB-containing lipoproteins in the intima, oxidation, uptake by macrophages (foam cells) and inflammation; LDL is a causal factor of ASCVD.
5. Laboratory monitoring: lipid profile, non-HDL cholesterol, apoB, Lp(a); LDL targets by risk level.
